fatal_errors: The proposed acid-dealloying/Pt-shell intervention is unrelated to the target closed-loop high-throughput synthesis, post-ageing screening, machine-learning prediction, Bayesian optimisation, and inverse-analysis campaign.

The starting material is incorrectly assumed to be a homogeneous high-entropy solid solution; the target fresh catalysts commonly contained agglomerates of fine particles and spanned five- to nineteen-element supported formulations.
The claimed enhanced M–N bonding has no physical basis in the proposed acid-etching treatment because no nitrogen-introduction step is specified.

None of the cited evidence demonstrates acid dealloying, Pt-rich-shell formation, or durability in water- and NO-containing automotive exhaust. The evidence concerns synthesis control, nitrogen-doped ORR electrocatalysts, and high-entropy-oxide OER catalysts.
The hypothesis does not address the target's severe 900 °C cyclic lean/rich ageing regime, which is central to the durability problem.
Forming a Pt-rich surface does not by itself establish reduced total platinum-group-metal consumption; no lower-PGM comparator or mass-normalized performance criterion is included.
explanation: The response recognizes the broad automotive-catalyst objective and proposes a testable treated-versus-untreated comparison, but it does not reconstruct the target intervention, mechanism, conditions, or performance framework. The target discovered composition and solvothermal-process combinations by iteratively optimizing post-ageing activity, with beneficial Cu–Pt electronic reconstruction and hydrocarbon-coupled NO reduction under a specified multicomponent feed. The generated hypothesis instead introduces unsupported acid dealloying, a Pt-rich core–shell structure, poisoning resistance, and M–N bonding. Its baseline omits both the Pd/Al2O3 benchmark and random-search baseline, and its experiment lacks the severe ageing protocol, species-resolved light-off metrics, and predictive-versus-random hit-rate test. Although XPS and TEM/EDS could verify whether dealloying produces surface enrichment, the cited literature does not validate the proposed intervention in the relevant catalytic environment, making this an insufficiently supported alternative rather than a reconstruction.
